articles.title: Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan activate Mecca Pact amid war with Houthis - Middle East Eye
articles.summary: Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan activate Mecca Pact amid war with Houthis  Middle East Eye
articles.full_text:
Turkey and Pakistan said they will undertake a "rapid deployment" of troops to Saudi Arabia as part of their new mutual defence alliance, the Mecca Pact, in a move that could deepen the Houthis' isolation in the region.
The announcement on Monday came after representatives of the three countries held an emergency meeting in Riyadh where they condemned recent attacks on Saudi Arabia, in particular those targeting the holy cities of Mecca and Medina, without mentioning the Houthis by name.
The trio "reaffirmed their unequivocal rejection of any attack or threat against the Kingdom's security and territorial integrity", they said in a joint statement.
They also agreed "to move immediately to the practical implementation of the collective defence commitments and to take the necessary measures to provide the agreed military forces and capabilities and ensure their rapid deployment in the Kingdom".
The meeting came as Yemeni government forces backed by Saudi Arabia launched a large-scale offensive whose mission the government said is to retake all the territory the Houthis conquered in 12 years of war.
It's unclear what immediate tactical impact Pakistan and Turkey's deployment to Saudi Arabia will have on the war.
Pakistan already has tens of thousands of troops in the kingdom. Reuters reported last week that Pakistan sent four plane loads of weapons to the port city of Aden to support the Saudi-backed government.
A western official in the Gulf told Middle East Eye that Pakistani personnel are already deployed in southern Yemen, although it's not clear if they are there as part of the Saudi military on contract or the Pakistani military.
Symbolism
But the timing of the announcement, with the offensive against the Houthis underway, carries deep symbolic weight.
A separate western official in the Gulf told MEE that Riyadh wanted to ensure it had "international buy-in" to launch a counter-offensive against the Houthis.
Pakistan is the Muslim world's only nuclear-armed state. It has also served as a mediator between Iran and the US, trying to pitch itself as an honest broker.
Turkey is a Nato member that has positioned itself as a rival to Israel, which is unpopular in the Arab and Muslim world because of its war on Gaza, which the United Nations and human rights experts have called a genocide.
By invoking the Mecca Pact, Saudi Arabia is able to underscore that it has the support of the wider region in its counter-offensive against the Houthis.
Last week, Saudi Arabia also hosted UAE Vice President Mansour bin Zayed, in a bid to show unity against the Houthis.
Also on Monday, Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman hosted Democratic Senator Chris Murphy for a two-hour conversation, the US politician said.
Murphy was one of the sharpest critics of the war in Yemen before a 2022 UN-backed ceasefire was reached. That agreement collapsed in July after the Houthis began attacking Saudi vessels in the Red Sea. Two months later, the Houthis launched an offensive down the Red Sea coast.
Yemeni forces backed by Saudi Arabia said on Monday that they had retaken most of the coastal territory the Houthis conquered.

articles.title: 2034 World Cup: Saudi Arabia puts $2.5bn NEOM stadium on hold amid infrastructure review - businessday.ng
articles.summary: 2034 World Cup: Saudi Arabia puts $2.5bn NEOM stadium on hold amid infrastructure review  businessday.ng
articles.full_text:
Saudi Arabia has put plans for a $2.5 billion stadium intended to host matches at the 2034 FIFA World Cup on hold, as the kingdom evaluates some of its ambitious projects under its Vision 2030 economic diversification programme.
The 46,000-seat NEOM Stadium, planned as one of the tournament’s venues, is listed as on hold with no completion date in data from MEED Projects, according to Reuters. Two sources familiar with the project also said plans to build the stadium had been shelved indefinitely.
The futuristic venue was designed to be built about 350 metres above ground within The Line, a 160 kilometer steel-and-glass development that forms part of the wider NEOM project.
Saudi Arabia was officially named host of the 2034 FIFA World Cup after its bid was ratified by acclamation on December 11, 2024, at an Extraordinary FIFA Congress in Zurich, Switzerland. The kingdom was the sole bidding candidate.
Read Also: FIFA confirms Saudi Arabia as host for 2034 World Cup amid controversy
The tournament will be the third men’s FIFA World Cup hosted in the Asian Football Confederation (AFC) region, after South Korea and Japan in 2002 and Qatar in 2022. It will also be the first 48-team World Cup hosted by a single nation.
NEOM project faces reprioritisation
The decision comes as Saudi Arabia reassesses some of its largest development projects under Vision 2030, an ambitious programme aimed at diversifying the economy and reducing its dependence on oil.
Yasir Al-Rumayyan, governor of the Public Investment Fund, which owns NEOM, said in April that The Line was no longer a priority and was not essential to deliver before 2030, although he denied that projects had been cancelled.
The NEOM Stadium was originally conceived as an elevated arena within The Line and formed part of Saudi Arabia’s plans to showcase the kingdom’s futuristic infrastructure during the World Cup.
NEOM and the Saudi government’s media office did not respond to requests for comment on the stadium. Saudi Arabia’s Ministry of Sports referred questions to the World Cup 2034 Hosting Higher Authority.
The authority said substantial construction milestones for the tournament were already being delivered but did not directly address the NEOM Stadium or its reported cost.
$22.7bn World Cup infrastructure programme
Saudi Arabia plans to stage the tournament across five host cities; Riyadh, Jeddah, Al Khobar, Abha and NEOM.
The kingdom plans to build or renovate 15 stadiums across the five cities, comprising 10 new venues and five major renovations, alongside major transport and infrastructure projects. MEED Projects estimates the total value of World Cup-related projects at $22.7 billion.
Despite the NEOM Stadium being put on hold, other major venues are progressing. The Prince Mohammed Bin Salman Stadium in Qiddiya, for example, has advanced with major construction and recently secured a $221 million mechanical, electrical and plumbing contract.
Saudi Arabia’s 2034 World Cup is a major component of its global sports strategy, which has seen the Public Investment Fund invest heavily in football and other sports as part of Vision 2030.
Financial and geopolitical pressures
The decision to put the NEOM Stadium on hold comes amid wider financial and geopolitical pressures facing the kingdom.
Saudi Arabia is dealing with disruptions to energy shipments and security risks linked to the regional conflict, including attacks by Iran-backed Houthi forces, while weaker oil activity has added pressure to the economy.
Reuters reported that Saudi Arabia’s Ministry of Finance expects a wider fiscal deficit and a 3.6 percent contraction in real GDP this year.
The developments have increased scrutiny of the kingdom’s spending commitments under Vision 2030, particularly its large-scale giga-projects designed to transform the economy and reduce its reliance on oil.
The World Cup remains a major pillar of that strategy, with Saudi Arabia continuing to invest in football infrastructure even as some of its most ambitious development projects are delayed, downsised or reprioritised.

Turkiye, Pakistan agree to military deployment to Saudi Arabia
Turkiye, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia have agreed to activate “deterrence measures” under a mutual defence pact and rapidly deploy forces to the Gulf kingdom to counter attacks by Yemen’s Houthis.
The decision was announced on Monday after the three countries’ defence and foreign ministers held an emergency meeting in Riyadh. It marked the first time the alliance – known as the Mecca Alliance for Defence – has been invoked since it was signed on August 7.
The agreement declares that an attack on any of the three nations will be treated as an attack on all, mirroring a central provision of NATO’s founding treaty.
“The committee agreed to activate collective deterrence measures, within the framework of the Alliance, in response to the attacks and all those responsible for them,” Khalid bin Salman, Saudi Arabia’s defence minister, said in a social media post.
He said the alliance had “reaffirmed the solidarity and unity of our countries, in confronting the heinous attacks against the Kingdom, and holy sites”.
A separate joint statement published by Pakistan’s Foreign Ministry said the three countries would “provide the agreed military forces and capabilities and ensure their rapid deployment” to Saudi Arabia.
The commitments, the joint statement said, would be carried out under “approved arrangements” and in accordance with each country’s laws.
The announcements came hours after forces aligned with Yemen’s internationally recognised government launched a counteroffensive to retake territory the Iran-aligned Houthis captured last month. The Yemeni forces, who are backed by Saudi Arabia, said they have retaken the port city of Mocha on the Red Sea and are now in control of the strategic Bab al-Mandeb strait.
The Saudi-led coalition has confirmed its participation in the Yemeni government offensive, saying 100 of its fighter jets are providing air support.
The Houthis, meanwhile, claimed an attack on the King Khalid International airport in Riyadh and the Aramco refinery in coastal Rabigh.
The group also said it hit a series of sites, including an airport, an airbase and other critical locations.
There was no confirmation from Riyadh on the Houthi claim.
Mecca defence pact
The Mecca Defence Alliance emerged as a response to intensifying conflicts in the region, triggered by the United States and Israel’s war on Iran.
The defence pact was signed in August, shortly before the Houthis launched their offensive in Yemen, which has included attacks against Saudi targets.
The three members of the alliance combined have nearly 1.4 million active troops, about 3,400 military aircraft, 6,000 tanks and more than 340 naval assets, according to the 2026 Global Firepower Index.
The agreement initially offered few details about each country’s military obligations, though steps to formalise the alliance followed.
After the Houthis fired a barrage of missiles towards Saudi Arabia in early September, Pakistani Defence Minister Khawaja Asif said an attack on the kingdom could set the pact in motion.
“If there is unprovoked aggression, or a spillover of whatever is happening in Yemen into Saudi Arabia, definitely the Mecca agreement will become operational,” Asif told Geo News, a Pakistani outlet.
Until Monday, however, the alliance had taken no action. Analysts had said that Pakistan and Turkiye were reluctant to abandon their roles as mediators in the US-Israel war on Iran.
Abdulaziz Alghashian, a senior non-resident fellow at the Gulf International Forum, said the decision to activate the Mecca defence pact will have a major impact on security in the region.
“The Houthi attacks and provocations in recent weeks and months really hastened the Mecca alliance, inspired it, even,” Alghashian told Al Jazeera. They “helped” push forward its structure, he said.
Alghashian said the episode also offered a glimpse of a regional security architecture taking shape.
“A lot of the times we keep talking about regional security architecture, it’s one of these very fancy words,” he said. “A lot of the times, it’s hollow, and not many people know what it means in detail. But I think now, we’re beginning to see how this is fleshed out. It’s a critical juncture in the history of the region.”

articles.title: Why haven’t Israel and Saudi Arabia normalized relations? - Unpacked
articles.summary: Why haven’t Israel and Saudi Arabia normalized relations?  Unpacked
articles.full_text:
When the passengers from FlyDubai Flight 1073 finally entered Israeli airspace after an attempted hijacking, some observers were surprised to see them aboard another FlyDubai plane rather than on Israeli aircraft.
This was no accident.
After the flight made an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia, Israel reportedly asked Saudi authorities for permission to send its own aircraft to pick up its citizens. Saudi Arabia allegedly denied the request, instead insisting that the passengers complete their journey on another FlyDubai plane.
The refusal highlighted the ongoing strain between Israel and one of the region’s most influential powers. Yet just three years ago, the two countries appeared to be moving toward establishing formal diplomatic relations in the wake of Israel’s agreements with four other Arab nations under the Abraham Accords. And with a shared foe in Iran and the Houthis, one might expect Israel and Saudi Arabia to have found more common ground.
So what makes the Israeli-Saudi relationship so complicated?
1. The future for Palestinians
Saudi Arabia has long tied normalization — establishing formal diplomatic relations — with Israel to Palestinian statehood. But before October 7, 2023, there were signs that a deal might be possible without an independent Palestinian state already in place. In September 2023, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman said normalization was getting “closer” every day, while emphasizing that the Palestinian issue remained important. Saudi Arabia had also permitted flights to and from Israel to cross its airspace, and the two countries had quietly cooperated on security matters.
The negotiations weren’t just about Israel and Saudi Arabia. They were part of a broader bargain with Washington: Saudi Arabia sought U.S. security guarantees and help developing a civilian nuclear program, with normalization as part of the package. For Riyadh, establishing ties with Israel offered a potential route to a stronger American security commitment.
Then came October 7. Disrupting a potential Israeli-Saudi agreement was one of Hamas’s aims, according to then-President Joe Biden. The attack and the ensuing war in Gaza put normalization talks on ice.
Saudi Arabia has since hardened its public position, reiterating that no normalization would happen without an independent Palestinian state. Alongside France, the kingdom also led a diplomatic initiative in 2025 urging other countries to recognize Palestinian statehood — a move Israel strongly opposed.
Palestinian statehood was firmly back at the center of the negotiations.
2. Common ground
Israel and Saudi Arabia do have one major interest in common: limiting Iran’s regional influence and the power of groups it backs, including Hezbollah in Lebanon and the Houthis in Yemen.
The U.S. has worked to turn those shared concerns into closer security cooperation, quietly facilitating intelligence sharing between Israel and Arab countries. That effort paid dividends in April 2024, when Israel and its partners intercepted what Israeli officials said was 99% of the drones and missiles Iran launched at Israel — thanks in part to Saudi-provided intelligence.
Saudi Arabia’s response to the Israeli-Iranian conflict has reflected its own security concerns. The kingdom criticized Israel’s strikes during the 12-day war in 2025. But after the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran began in February 2026, Saudi Arabia itself faced repeated Iranian missile and drone attacks. In March, it condemned those attacks and ordered Iran’s military attaché and four other embassy staff members to leave.
Still, the idea that the Saudis are quietly giving Israel a green light to attack Iran is more complicated than it seems. As CSIS analyst Michael Ratney explains, Saudi Arabia must weigh the damage to the Iranian regime against the regional instability and economic harm the war could bring. A weaker Iran may serve Saudi interests, but a wider war threatens the kingdom’s infrastructure, investment plans and security.
Ditto with Lebanon. Israel and Saudi Arabia both want Hezbollah disarmed and its influence diminished. But while Israel has been willing to go on the offensive, Saudi Arabia has emphasized diplomacy and strengthening the Lebanese state.
Even when the two countries don’t see eye to eye on how to address shared threats, backchannels remain open. According to a September report by Kan News, Israel began providing intelligence on the Houthis to Saudi Arabia through the United States, following a Saudi request for American assistance.
3. Broader regional dynamics
When it comes to the wider region, things get even more complicated.
Saudi concerns extend beyond Iran and its allies. The kingdom also worries that Israel’s military actions could throw the region into further turmoil, threatening Saudi security and economic ambitions.
That concern was especially clear when Israel targeted Hamas leaders in Qatar in September 2025. Saudi Arabia condemned the strike as a “criminal act and a flagrant violation of international laws and norms,” and pledged its full support for Qatar.
And to add another layer of complexity, Saudi Arabia has been feuding with the United Arab Emirates, one of Israel’s regional partners. Their competing approaches to Yemen — with Saudi Arabia backing a unified state and the UAE supporting southern separatists — have brought that friction into the open.
For its part, Israel has sharply criticized Saudi Arabia’s alignment with Turkey and Qatar. Its concerns deepened in August 2026, when Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan signed a mutual defense pact declaring that an armed attack on one would be treated as an attack on all. Analysts at the International Institute for Strategic Studies describe Israel as suspicious of the agreement, particularly given its growing rivalry with Turkey.
4. Help in an emergency
With Saudi public opinion toward Israel strained by the war in Gaza, the shaken passengers of Flight 1073 might have expected a cold reception when they stepped off the plane at Prince Sultan bin Abdulaziz International Airport in Tabuk.
Instead, passengers who spoke to news outlets described a warm welcome from Saudi airport staff. “They gave everyone medical treatment, they gave us food and something to drink, sweets for the kids,” one passenger told CBC.
The warm reception didn’t erase the diplomatic limits: Saudi Arabia still refused to allow Israeli military aircraft to retrieve the passengers. But those limits didn’t prevent Saudi staff from caring for the people who had landed on their doorstep.
Diplomacy might be on the rocks, but in a moment of need, humanity shone through.

Depending on where you live, you may have seen fuel prices drop over the weekend, but that wasn't because Republicans are finally winning the senseless war they started with Iran. No, it's mostly because the governors of Georgia and Ohio suspended their states' gas taxes, while governors in other states have found short-term solutions for temporarily making diesel less expensive. Meanwhile, over in the Strait of Hormuz, the Wall Street Journal reports Iran has increased its attacks on oil tankers attempting to transit the strait, slowing oil exports yet again.
According to the WSJ, crude oil shipments had largely returned to prewar levels after a series of U.S. strikes took out Iran's radar and communications abilities along the strait. That lull in hostilities, combined with Gulf countries working overtime to find alternative routes that avoid the strait, briefly allowed oil exports to surge. But much like Georgia's suddenly lower gas prices, Iran losing its targeting capabilities was only temporary. Since September 28, UK Maritime Trade Operations data shows Iran has hit seven ships traveling through Hormuz, and it appears Iran struck an eighth ship on Sunday, as well. As the WSJ explained:
Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps navy issued a warning to ships planning to use the U.S.-backed route through the strait on Saturday, saying that they would be targeted and destroyed. "Don't trust U.S. Navy and don't use south corridor at all and don't put your life in danger," a radio message transmitted on a public shipping channel and reviewed by The Wall Street Journal said.
The renewed attacks may already be taking a toll, with early signs that oil flows are beginning to slow, analysts say. Firm data comes with a lag, because many ships are operating without their transponders switched on to avoid becoming targets.
All seven vessels were attacked near the narrowest part of the Hormuz strait, according to UKMTO.
Iran's targeting is improving
Ideally, the oppressive regime running Iran would be getting weaker as the war stretches past its seventh month, but according to one U.S. official the WSJ spoke with, that's not the case. Instead, they're reportedly getting better at targeting ships in the strait, undermining Republican claims that the U.S. controls the strait and threatening to send fuel prices even higher:
Iran's ability to target ships has also improved in recent weeks, adding to the risks in the strait, according to a U.S. official. The U.S. several weeks ago said it would strike Iranian oil tankers in response to Tehran's attacks, but it has since backed off that effort after Iran unleashed a wave of missiles at a U.S. air base in Jordan, the official said.
The new strikes expose the fragility of the recovery in oil flows and come as President Trump, who has claimed full U.S. control over Hormuz, weighs renewed military action against Iran.
At the moment, AAA reports the average gas price in the U.S. is still $4.37 a gallon, while the average gallon of diesel sits at $6.32. Brent Crude, meanwhile, is still trading at more than $100 a barrel, and if Iran continues to target tankers with increased precision, analysts say to expect Brent to stay over $100 through the rest of this year and on into 2028. "The step-up in attacks on ships highlights how the current equilibrium in the oil market is fragile and could easily be shattered," Capital Economics senior economist Hamad Hussain told the WSJ. "This would especially be the case if there is further escalation and energy infrastructure is targeted."
Putin continuing his invasion of Ukraine isn't helping with global oil prices, either, with ABC News reporting that Ukrainian counterattacks have knocked out half of Russia's refining capacity. Meanwhile, NBC News reports Yemen and Saudi Arabia still have their hands full with the Houthi rebels who took control of the Bab al-Mandeb Strait and recently struck an Aramco facility in Riyadh. Oh, and on top of that, Reuters reports China just suspended fuel exports. Fun!
Higher gas prices aren't going anywhere
According to another analyst the WSJ spoke with, the pullback in response to Iran's attacks is already starting. From the WSJ:
Rory Johnston, founder of oil research firm Commodity Context, said he has seen a potential pullback in recent days and estimates that flows are down by two million to three million barrels a day, though those initial totals could be revised higher as better information becomes available.
"The recent pace of flows, while impressive, has never been sustainable and has already come at great expense," Johnston said. Part of the surge may reflect exporters rushing barrels out before a feared new escalation, he said. Gulf oil producers are shelling out between $30 million and $40 million for a round trip shuttle run in and out of Hormuz—or $15 to $20 a barrel, according to shipbrokers, before insurance costs.
Even if the U.S. somehow wins a war it currently appears to be losing, don't expect higher gas prices to drop overnight, either. Speaking publicly for the first time since the war began at the end of Feburary, Reuters reports that Saudi Aramco CEO Amin Nasser told London's Energy Intelligence Forum, "Until Hormuz fully re-opens and confidence returns, the crude reality is that pressure at both ends of the barrel will intensify. Even then, replenishing inventories while meeting demand could take up to two years." Nasser also added, "The system is already straining."
So basically, expect gas to stay expensive as long as this war drags on and probably several years after it ends. We aren't to the point where it makes financial sense to sell a perfectly good car for something more efficient — if you drive 21,000 miles a year and average 20 mpg, $6 a gallon is only $525 a month — but if you have to replace your current car anyway, you may want to take a look at hybrids or EVs. Alternatively, just do what I did and buy a motorcycle from a chainsaw company. Trust me when I tell you expensive gas isn't so bad when you're averaging over 50 mpg.

Planned 46,000-seat venue inside The Line put on hold indefinitely as kingdom reassesses giga-projects; Saudi Arabia is developing or renovating 15 World Cup venues
RIYADH/DUBAI: Saudi Arabia is quietly shelving plans to build one of its most ambitious stadiums for the 2034 FIFA World Cup, two sources familiar with the matter said, after delays and downscaling of the futuristic development housing it.
The proposed 46,000-seat $2.5 billion NEOM Stadium was designed as an elevated arena within The Line, the planned 160-kilometre steel-and-glass city that forms part of the wider NEOM development.
MEED Projects, a Dubai-based construction intelligence platform, estimates the stadium would cost $2.5 billion and now lists the project as “on hold”, with no completion date.
The Line was originally one of the flagship projects under Saudi Arabia's Vision 2030 economic diversification programme. Public Investment Fund Governor Yasir Al-Rumayyan said in April that The Line was no longer a priority and was not essential for completion before 2030, although he denied that projects had been cancelled.
NEOM and the Saudi government media office did not respond to requests for comment.
The World Cup 2034 Hosting Higher Authority said substantial construction milestones for the tournament were already being delivered but did not specifically address the status of the NEOM Stadium.
Saudi Arabia is planning to build or renovate 15 World Cup venues across five cities alongside dozens of training facilities for the 2034 tournament, which will be the first edition of the expanded 48-team competition hosted by a single country.
MEED estimates the combined value of the stadium projects at $22.7 billion, with the remaining venues and facilities at various stages of development and expected to be completed between 2026 and 2033.
The shelving of the NEOM venue comes as Saudi Arabia reassesses some of its expensive giga-projects. Construction of The Mukaab, the cube-shaped skyscraper at the centre of Riyadh's New Murabba development, was suspended earlier this year.
The PIF has also been shifting its investment strategy towards projects offering more immediate financial returns.
Saudi Arabia is simultaneously facing fiscal pressure from the Iran war, which has disrupted energy shipments and damaged critical infrastructure. The Ministry of Finance last week projected a wider fiscal deficit this year and a 3.6% contraction in real GDP following a decline in oil activity.
Other World Cup projects continue to move ahead. The Aramco Stadium in Al Khobar is expected to be completed by the end of 2026 and host its first match in January, while work is progressing on other planned venues.

Saudi Arabia has quietly shelved plans to build the futuristic NEOM Stadium, which was slated to host matches at the 2034 World Cup.
The 46,000-seat stadium was supposed to be built as part of the 170km-long mega city, The Line. The project was announced by Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman in 2021 but has been beset by issues and spiralling costs ever since.
According to a report from earlier this year, just 2.4km of foundation work has actually been completed for the ambitious project, which has also been accused of human rights abuses, with native Huwaitat tribe forcefully removed from their land.
Saudi Arabia was announced as the host of the 2034 World Cup by FIFA back in December 2024, with NEOM listed as one of the venues. The Saudi 2034 website promises it will be "built as a living laboratory – an accelerator of human progress", "a new model for livability" and "a future global hub".

The Middle Eastern country's commitment to sport has been wavering in recent years, with the country's decision to withdraw funding for LIV Golf in April a clear sign. With the World Cup coming to Saudi Arabia as part of the country's wider tourism goals, stadium infrastructure is a necessity.

Pakistan and Turkey meanwhile pledged to deploy troops to Saudi Arabia under a new mutual defence pact following weeks of Houthi attacks, as Riyadh and its Yemeni government allies began an ambitious push aimed at retaking all territory held by the group.
The Yemeni military said it carried out more than 1,000 strikes and began an offensive against the Houthi-held capital, Sanaa, while the Saudi-led coalition supporting the internationally recognised government said 100 warplanes flew sorties at dawn.
Turki Al-Malki, spokesman for the Saudi-led coalition said on X that its naval forces had hit “military targets” belonging to the Houthis in Hodeida on the Red Sea coast.
They “destroyed weapons depots, facilities storing booby-trapped boats and naval mines” and had “thwarted a planned attack” targeting waterways in the southern Red Sea, he said.
Loud explosions rattled Riyadh on Monday evening as the fighting escalated, and a Houthi spokesman said the group had hit the Saudi capital’s King Khalid International Airport as well as an Aramco refinery and other targets in the kingdom’s south.
The government announced on Sunday the lofty goal of retaking all Houthi territory – home to most of Yemen’s population, and much of it held for more than a decade.
Last month the Iran-backed group seized swathes of coastline along the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandab Strait, a chokepoint for oil and cargo shipping, in Yemen’s deadliest fighting in years.
The Houthis have also been attacking neighbouring Saudi Arabia since Yemen’s civil war flared back to life, and have declared a maritime blockade on its ships.
On Monday, representatives of Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey held an emergency meeting in Riyadh under the auspices of a joint defence agreement signed in August committing them to come to each other’s aid in the event of any attack.
They also agreed “to take the necessary measures to provide the agreed military forces and capabilities and ensure their rapid deployment in the Kingdom”.
The statement did not specify what sort of role the troops would fill once in Saudi Arabia.
A spokesman for UN secretary-general Antonio Guterres said he was “deeply concerned by the sharp escalation in fighting”, and condemned “the continued Houthi cross-border attacks” on Saudi Arabia”.
Global oil system ‘straining’
Houthi attacks have also targeted Saudi oil infrastructure, as well as its tankers in the Red Sea.
A source in the Saudi energy sector told AFP that an attack Sunday had again halted pumping by the East-West pipeline to the Red Sea, a key conduit for the kingdom’s exports since Iran blockaded the Strait of Hormuz at the start of the wider Middle East war.
Crude prices had already been soaring as a result of the Middle East war, before the Houthis began targeting the world’s largest oil exporter.
Saudi Aramco chief executive Amin Nasser warned on Monday that global oil stockpiles were “scarily thin” owing to the war.
“The system is already straining,” Nasser told the Energy Intelligence Forum in London.
Mokha fighting
Yemeni military sources said Monday that pro-government forces had cut off the only supply route to the Houthi-held city of Mocha, but stopped short of confirming an official announcement of the port’s recapture.
While the war in Yemen predates the broader Middle East war that began with US-Israeli strikes on Iran, it has become its most active front in recent weeks. According to UN figures, the fighting has displaced more than 184,000 people.
Yemen’s civil war began broke out in 2014, with the Saudis intervening the following March, but fighting was paused by a 2022 ceasefire that held until July of this year.

Yemen's internationally recognized government says it has launched a major military operation against Iran-backed Houthi rebels
Yemen's internationally recognized government has announced a major military operation against the Iran -backed Houthi rebels as they advance in the outskirts of a key city.
Meanwhile, the Iranian parliament speaker who was the lead negotiator in direct talks with the U.S. earlier this year says Washington recently put forward proposals via a mediator, without details. And Israeli strikes have killed at least two people in Gaza.
Here is the latest news from the Middle East on Sunday. Full coverage is available here.
Rashad al-Alimi, head of the ruling Presidential Leadership Council, made the declaration as the Iran-backed rebels advanced in the outskirts of a key southwestern city, Taiz.
Speaking from Saudi Arabia, he said the operation aims at “recovering the remaining territories” controlled by the Houthis, who made their largest land grab in recent years last month when they seized Yemen’s Red Sea coast and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
Al-Alimi called for the international community to provide support to his Saudi-backed government.
The Houthis have launched a major offensive in recent days against government forces and their allies on the outskirts of Taiz, disrupting a major road linking the city to the port city of Aden, the seat of al-Alimi’s government. The rebels have besieged Taiz for more than a decade.
Earlier, the Houthis said airstrikes hit the capital, Sanaa, overnight, without giving details. The Yemeni military, backed by Riyadh, claimed responsibility, saying it struck “vital targets” in Sanaa as well as the northern province of Saada on the border with Saudi Arabia.
The escalation between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis has revived Yemen’s civil war after a four-year ceasefire.
The United States recently put forward proposals through a mediator, Iran's parliament speaker, Mohammad Bagher Qalibaf, told an open session of Parliament, without details.
U.S. President Donald Trump last week said he rejected Iran’s latest peace offer because it’s not good enough. Qalibaf, the lead negotiator in rare direct talks with the U.S. earlier this year, said Americans “say something different in the media.”
Qalibaf said “the era of dragging out time and dictating unilateral demands is over” and that Iran's seven conditions for fully reopening the Strait of Hormuz remain.
Separately, Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi told ambassadors and chargés d’affaires of foreign missions in Tehran that “if they seek diplomatic avenues, we remain ready to reach a fair and honorable solution through diplomacy to end this war." But he warned that any renewed military confrontation would bring a stronger response.
Araghchi also rejected a U.S. claim that the Iranian delegation had been expelled from the U.S. days after the annual U.N. gathering of world leaders, where Iran proposed a deal to the U.S. that was turned down. He said Iran had returned according to a previously arranged schedule.
Iran’s oil minister resigned and President Masoud Pezeshkian accepted his resignation, state television reported. Pezeshkian appointed Hamid Bovard as caretaker oil minister following the resignation of Mohsen Paknejad.
The reason for the resignation was not immediately clear. It came as Iran’s oil exports face intense pressure from tightened U.S. sanctions and a naval blockade.
Iran’s ability to export oil is a crucial source of government revenue. Tehran has demanded that Washington lift sanctions on its oil sales and end the blockade as part of negotiations over reopening the Strait of Hormuz.
An Israeli strike on a civilian vehicle killed one Palestinian and wounded at least 11 others, according to health officials at the Aqsa Martyrs Hospital, where the casualties were taken. Israel’s military said it targeted a known Hamas militant.
Later, a Turkish aid agency, the Deniz Feneri Association, said one of its volunteers was killed in an Israeli attack in Gaza. Israel's military said it “eliminated” a Hamas militant whom it described as the aid group's director.
Palestinians in Gaza have reported a surge in Israeli fire and airstrikes across the enclave over the past month. Israel says it is targeting Hamas and other militants who pose a threat, and in response to ceasefire violations, including occasional attacks.
Israeli strikes have killed at least 1,445 Palestinians in Gaza since a ceasefire was reached with the Hamas militant group nearly a year ago, according to the territory’s Health Ministry. Its figures are seen as generally reliable by U.N. agencies and independent experts. It doesn’t give a breakdown of civilians and militants. Seven Israeli soldiers have been killed in Gaza since the ceasefire.
A projectile struck a tanker on the Strait of Hormuz, damaging the engine room, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations Center said.
It was not immediately clear who launched the attack or when it was carried out. The UKMTO said the crew was reportedly safe.
The monitor in a separate report said three tankers were struck on Saturday while transiting the strait, noting that attacks on the Omani side of the strait continue. That's where the U.S. military has been guiding vessels.
Overall ship traffic on the strait has improved but remains below prewar levels, as do shipments of energy products, even though Iran has lost its near-complete grip on the crucial waterway due to the U.S. Navy’s efforts. That, along with various pipelines, has allowed Gulf countries to restore oil exports to nearly prewar levels.
The Houthi military spokesperson, Brig. Gen. Yahya Saree, said the rebels fired missiles and drones at Saudi oil facilities.
In a prerecorded statement, Saree claimed to have targeted facilities of the Saudi state-run Aramco oil company, in the capital, Riyadh, and the Kurais area, which hosts a massive facility 150 kilometers (90 miles) southeast of Riyadh.
He didn’t say when it occurred, provide further details or offer evidence supporting his claim. A fire broke out at an Aramco oil refinery on Saturday, with no details released on the cause.

articles.full_text:
Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces on Monday seized key positions on the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, military sources said, in an effort to reverse Houthi advances and clear the vital waterway.
The government forces have taken large parts of Dhubab district, which overlooks the strait and are asserting full control over the area with heavy air support from a Saudi-led coalition, three military sources and one government source told Reuters.
Houthi-aligned media earlier denied that government forces had made advances in the area, describing such claims as "completely untrue."
Meanwhile, the Houthis late Sunday advanced onto sections of the mountain road to the major city of Taiz, besieging government forces there, according to five government sources. One other government source denied the road had been cut.
Fighting has raged along several front lines in Yemen for weeks after a dormant civil war erupted in a spillover from the U.S.-Iran conflict, with the Houthis seeking to control the vital Bab el-Mandeb Strait and firing missiles and drones at Saudi cities and infrastructure.
With Gulf energy exports already restricted by Iran's closure of the Hormuz Strait, the fighting in Yemen has threatened another major oil export route, pushing up global prices and raising new risks in a region already aflame.
The internationally recognized Yemeni government announced Sunday the launch of its offensive to recapture territory, with President Rashad al-Alimi swearing to fight "until the country is liberated from the grip of the terrorist militia."
Saudi Arabia, which arms and trains Yemeni government forces, is backing the military campaign with air power and has sought logistical help from allies to push back the Houthis, restore free traffic in the Red Sea, and end the group's attacks on its territory.
Riyadh said Monday it had attacked hundreds of targets in Yemen to provide air cover for the Bab el-Mandeb Strait and Yemeni ground forces.
The Yemeni government said it had launched attacks on several fronts including in the province of Sanaa, the Yemeni capital.
While the war has raged on several front lines in Yemen, the heaviest fighting has been in the southwest, both in the coastal area near the strait and in the hills around Taiz, where the Houthis have been battling to surround government forces.
Last week, Houthi attacks damaged a culvert on the Taiz-Aden road, making it impassable.
On Sunday night the group's fighters made new advances into the town of al-Turbah, sitting atop a high promontory on the road, five government military sources said, though another government source denied this.
A Houthi-run news agency Monday meanwhile cited a military source as saying that the group had driven government forces from the al-Mawasit district of Taiz province, reaching the home of Alimi, head of Yemen's interim presidential council.
Those fresh advances leave Taiz, Yemen's third-largest city with a population of over half a million and a garrison of thousands of government fighters, surrounded by Houthi forces, the government military sources said.
The city, nestled among Yemen's southern highlands, has been on the front lines since early in the civil war, often under Houthi shell and sniper fire.
Yemen's conflict began after the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa in 2014, prompting a Saudi-led coalition to intervene in the following year with an air campaign aimed at restoring the government and ousting the Iran-backed group.
The fighting quickly ground to a bloody stalemate, with most front lines stalled, leading to a major humanitarian crisis in what was already the poorest Arab state, until a ceasefire was agreed in 2022 that held until this summer.

The U.S. State Department has approved potential arms sales worth a combined $2.27 billion to Egypt, Kuwait and the United Arab Emirates, including missiles, defense support and precision-guidance equipment.
The largest of the three is a possible sale to the UAE of Advanced Precision Kill Weapon System-II guidance sections and related equipment at an estimated cost of $1.041 billion, the department said in a statement.
The UAE "has requested to buy up to ten thousand (10,000) Advanced Precision Kill Weapon System-II guidance sections consisting of a combination of air-to-air and air-to-ground configurations," it added.
For Egypt, the department approved a possible sale of Javelin missile systems at an estimated cost of $832 million.
Cairo has requested to buy up to 2,020 Javelin FGM-148F missiles, including 20 fly-to-buy missiles, and up to 200 Javelin Lightweight Command Launch Units, according to the notification.
For Kuwait, it approved a possible sale of Patriot missile repair and return services and related equipment at an estimated cost of $400 million.
The sale comes more than seven months into the Iran war, which began on Feb. 28 when the U.S. and Israel launched coordinated strikes on Iran.
Iran retaliated with attacks on U.S. bases in Bahrain, Qatar, the UAE, Kuwait, Jordan and Saudi Arabia.
The U.S. and Iran signed a framework agreement in June outlining immediate steps to restore freedom of navigation through the Strait of Hormuz and address Iran's nuclear program, but it expired in August without a final deal.

articles.title: Iran's Pezeshkian says negotiations with US 'meaningless'
articles.summary: Negotiations with the U.S. are "meaningless," Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said Monday, arguing that attacks continued even after talks, as little progress was achieved on e...
articles.full_text:
Negotiations with the U.S. are "meaningless," Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said Monday, arguing that attacks continued even after talks, as little progress was achieved on ending the Middle East war that began earlier this year.
"So far, they have attacked us three times after talks, and this shows that they are not seeking dialogue; rather, their goal is to overthrow the Islamic Republic of Iran," Pezeshkian was quoted as saying by the state news agency IRNA.
"With an enemy that every day resorts to assassination, sanctions, pressure and threats, and that breaks its commitments, negotiations are meaningless."
The Middle East war was started in late February by the U.S. and Israel when they launched a wave of surprise attacks on Iran, even as Washington and Tehran were in the midst of negotiations on Iran's nuclear program.
The warring parties agreed on a memorandum of understanding in June that spelled out a framework for a permanent resolution to the conflict but Iranian attacks on vessels in the Strait of Hormuz prompted a return to U.S. military operations.
Negotiations have effectively been at an impasse since then, and recent indirect talks between the U.S. and Iran on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly failed to produce a breakthrough.
Washington in recent weeks has dialled back military operations in favour of economic pressure, and has not struck Iran since Sept. 1.
On Sunday, Iran's top diplomat insisted the United States' war against the country would not be resolved by military means.
Vowing a stronger defense if any attacks resumed, Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said: "There is no military solution, nor any solution based on new sanctions."
"Only negotiations based on justice and fairness" could end the conflict, he added.
The U.S. and Israel have said the war is necessary to prevent Iran from acquiring nuclear weapons – a goal it has long denied pursuing – though the focus soon shifted to reopening the Strait of Hormuz after its closure sent shockwaves through world energy markets.
Iran has sought to impose its control over the vital shipping lane since the start of the war, striking vessels that attempt to transit without its authorisation.
The U.S. has imposed its own counterblockade of Iranian ports and has also struck vessels it accuses of violating it.
A tanker was struck while attempting to transit the waterway on Sunday while another turned back on Monday after being threatened with attack by Iranian forces, according to the British maritime agency UKMTO.

articles.title: UK security chief fails to secure Jerusalem consulate deal in Israel visit
articles.summary: Britain's national security adviser made an undisclosed visit to Israel last week but failed to reach a deal to prevent the closure of the U.K. Consulate in Israeli-occupied East J...
articles.full_text:
Britain's national security adviser made an undisclosed visit to Israel last week but failed to reach a deal to prevent the closure of the U.K. Consulate in Israeli-occupied East Jerusalem, three sources familiar with the talks said.
Jonathan Powell, whose visit has not been disclosed by Britain's government, held talks with Israeli officials but failed to reach an agreement to keep the consulate open, said the sources, who spoke on condition of anonymity.
Israel on Sept. 8 ordered Britain to close the East Jerusalem consulate within 30 days and remove its diplomats from the city, after Britain said it would ban goods made in illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.
France and Canada joined in the sanctions. Israel has not taken action against them.
The incident highlighted growing frustration among Israel's longtime allies over its unlawful settlements in the occupied West Bank, viewed by much of the world as illegal under international law.
The 30-day deadline for Britain to close the consulate runs out on Thursday. Two of the sources said talks were still ongoing, and while an agreement to keep it open was possible, it is unlikely one would be struck by the Thursday deadline.
Asked about Powell's visit and talks with London over the consulate, a spokesperson for Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar told Reuters that it would close on Thursday, as announced.
A U.K. government spokesperson had no immediate comment.
In announcing the sanctions, Britain said that Israel's actions were undermining the possibility of a two-state solution - the idea of a Palestinian state co-existing peacefully alongside Israel. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's government openly rejects the idea of Palestinian statehood.
Britain cited Israeli government-backed plans to expand illegal settlements and rising settler violence targeting Palestinians in the West Bank. The British sanctions are to take effect next year.
The British consulate, in the Sheikh Jarrah neighborhood of East Jerusalem, handles the country's relations with Palestinians in the city as well as in the West Bank and Gaza. It also provides consular services to Palestinians.
The British sanctions announcement and Israel's response marked a new low in the relationship between the once steadfast allies. Britain has repeatedly criticized Israel over its violations in the war in Gaza and over Israeli settler attacks on Palestinians.

articles.title: Pakistan rolls out fuel subsidies as oil prices squeeze households
articles.summary: Pakistan has rolled out a nationwide fuel subsidy scheme targeting motorcycle, rickshaw and small-car owners as rising global oil prices put pressure on working- and middle-income...
articles.full_text:
Pakistan has rolled out a nationwide fuel subsidy scheme targeting motorcycle, rickshaw and small-car owners as rising global oil prices put pressure on working- and middle-income households, the Prime Minister’s Office said.
Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif launched the Prime Minister’s Special Relief Scheme to provide targeted assistance to people who rely on their vehicles for work and daily transportation, particularly those who often fall outside conventional social assistance programs.
Under the scheme, eligible motorcycle, rickshaw and Qingqi users receive 500 Pakistani rupees ($1.78) in fuel relief per week through four tokens a month.
The government has removed an initial 5-liter minimum purchase requirement, meaning users can now receive the full Rs. 500 subsidy regardless of how much petrol they buy.
Owners of cars with engines of up to 800cc, meanwhile, receive a discount of Rs. 100 per liter on 10 liters every 10 days, with three subsidized tokens available each month.
The government also expanded eligibility for motorcycles, rickshaws and Qingqis from vehicles up to 15 years old to those up to 20 years old following public feedback. Vehicles registered on or after Jan. 1, 2006, can now qualify.
Eligible citizens can register free of charge through the government's 9771 SMS service, while a digital system links applicants' national identity, registered SIM cards and vehicle records to help prevent duplicate claims and misuse.
The Prime Minister’s Office said the program was developed rapidly despite Pakistan's limited fiscal space and was intended to shield vulnerable households from the impact of global energy price increases.
Sharif is personally overseeing the scheme, with the government saying further adjustments could be made in response to feedback from recipients.

articles.title: Italy’s Meloni moves to trademark voice amid AI deepfake fears
articles.summary: Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni has moved to trademark her voice across the EU in an effort to guard against its unauthorized use in AI-generated deepfakes. The application f...
articles.full_text:
Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni has moved to trademark her voice across the EU in an effort to guard against its unauthorized use in AI-generated deepfakes.
The application filed with the EU agency includes a four-second audio recording of Meloni repeating the phrase, in Italian, "Io sono Giorgia Meloni” ("I am Giorgia Meloni”), according to the EU office's records on Monday.
The filing, first reported by Italian daily La Repubblica, was confirmed by an Italian official who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak publicly.
Meloni’s move comes as governments, regulators and public figures grapple with the rapid spread of artificial intelligence tools capable of convincingly replicating voices and images.
The recorded phrase echoes Meloni’s famous declaration at a 2019 political rally: "I am Giorgia, I am a woman, I am a mother, I am Italian, I am Christian.” The slogan became widely known in Italy and inspired a viral dance remix. "Io sono Giorgia” was also the title of her 2021 autobiography.
Manipulated images of Meloni have repeatedly circulated online in recent years and have at times been passed off as authentic. Among them was a fake image showing her sitting on a bed in her underwear.
Meloni has warned that deepfakes can "deceive, manipulate and harm anyone,” urging users to verify online content before sharing it.
"I can defend myself, but many others cannot,” she said in May, after fake images of her surfaced online.
Pop star Taylor Swift was among the most prominent targets of deepfakes in 2024, after sexually explicit AI-generated images falsely depicting her spread widely online, fueling calls for stronger legal protections against unauthorized digital replicas.
Matthew McConaughey was one of the first major celebrities to use trademark registrations to secure rights to voice clips and motion elements.
Fellow actor Scarlett Johansson also raised concerns about AI-generated voices after objecting to an OpenAI chatbot voice that she said sounded "eerily similar” to her own. She had declined to participate in the project. OpenAI denied intentionally imitating Johansson’s voice and later withdrew the feature.
And in Japan last week, a court awarded legal protection to the human voice for the first time. The case involved a popular Japanese anime voice actor who demanded that TikTok close an account over its unauthorized use of an AI clone of his trademark baritone.
Italian media reported that even if Meloni's application is approved, the trademark will not automatically prevent AI-generated imitations of her voice. It could, however, provide an additional legal tool against unauthorized use.
The filing follows a separate legal battle launched by Meloni in 2024 against a man accused of creating and posting deepfake pornographic images using her likeness. The case remains pending before an Italian court.

articles.summary: U.S. President Donald Trump said on Monday that Washington was closely following a reported case of pneumonic plague in Russia as he also pledged to provide assistance. "We’re look...
articles.full_text:
U.S. President Donald Trump said on Monday that Washington was closely following a reported case of pneumonic plague in Russia as he also pledged to provide assistance.
"We’re looking at it very strongly. We just heard about it,” Trump told reporters at the White House before departing for a campaign rally in Nebraska.
"Years ago you could treat pneumonia easier, and the microbes and the germs have gotten stronger," he said.
"But we'll help them. We'll help them."
The U.S. State Department said earlier on Monday that it is monitoring reports of a fatal case of suspected pneumonic plague in Russia’s Irkutsk region with the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and other agencies.
Russian authorities have said the case involved pneumonia of unknown etiology and that no accidents were detected at a local anti-plague research institute.

articles.title: NATO prepares strategy for defeating potential Russian attack
articles.summary: NATO is readying a strategy on how to counter a potential Russian attack, with a top commander, Alexus Grynkewich, expected to elaborate on his "theory of victory" next week in Pol...
articles.full_text:
NATO is readying a strategy on how to counter a potential Russian attack, with a top commander, Alexus Grynkewich, expected to elaborate on his "theory of victory" next week in Poland, a spokesperson said Monday, as fears grow over the threat from Moscow.
"The Supreme Allied Commander Europe's theory of victory is simple: maintain NATO's advantage, which is consistent with and grounded upon the alliance's deterrence and defense plans," Colonel Martin O'Donnell, a spokesperson for the U.S. general, said.
"But given the unsettled and complex global security environment, we need to set conditions now to deter aggression and, if necessary, win if attacked," O'Donnell said, noting the theory sets out a framework to do just that.
He said that Grynkewich would speak about his ideas at a security conference in Warsaw next Monday.
The move from the top military commander comes as NATO seeks to send a message to Moscow to halt what Western officials say is a "hybrid" campaign of sabotage and interference against Ukraine's backers.
Fears have grown in recent months that the Kremlin is stepping up its actions after high-profile incidents, including the discovery of an explosive-laden drone at a German airport.
NATO traditionally closely guards its defense plans to counter any attack by Russia.

articles.title: Brazilian assets rally as Flavio Bolsonaro tops first-round vote
articles.summary: Brazilian assets were trading higher on Monday after right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, the son of ex-leader Jair Bolsonaro, came in first in the first round of Sunday's presiden...
articles.full_text:
Brazilian assets were trading higher on Monday after right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, the son of ex-leader Jair Bolsonaro, came in first in the first round of Sunday's presidential election.
The Bovespa benchmark stock index gained more than 8% and the country's currency strengthened against the U.S. dollar following the vote.
The eldest son of former President Jair Bolsonaro won 47% of the votes and will face leftist incumbent President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, who secured about 45% of the vote, in a runoff on Oct. 25. Polls had forecast Lula would lead the first round of voting by around three percentage points.
Investors cheered on Monday morning as Bolsonaro's strong showing was matched by gains for his allies in Congress. Analysts say a friendlier legislature would make it easier for him, if elected, to push through a pro-market agenda of tighter public spending, privatizations and tax cuts.
"Brazil wants change," Bolsonaro said on Sunday evening, heralding the "end of the era of (Lula's) Workers' Party."
Shares in retailer Magazine Luiza, stock exchange operator B3, lender BTG Pactual, homebuilder Cyrela and conglomerate Cosan jumped more than 20% each, putting them among the top gainers.
J.P. Morgan upgraded Brazil's equities to "overweight" on Monday, saying a more favorable political backdrop after recent election developments had improved the outlook for the region's largest market and could drive a period of outperformance.
Brazil's real currency strengthened more than 4% against the U.S. dollar in early trading, moving below 5.00 per greenback, from around 5.22 previously, in line with analyst forecasts and with the currency's performance four years ago when then-President Jair Bolsonaro did better than expected in the first-round vote against Lula.
The elder Bolsonaro went on to lose to Lula in the second round of that election and was subsequently convicted of trying to carry out a coup to overturn the result. The former president was sentenced to about 27 years in prison and is currently under house arrest.
Brazil's international debt also rallied on Monday, while broader fixed-income markets were jittery. The 2056 bond was up 1.4 cents on the dollar to bid at 93.5 cents, Tradeweb data showed.
Bolsonaro has pitched himself as a "more centered" version of his father to investors concerned about Brazil's burgeoning fiscal pressures.
"It remains to be seen whether the senator would ultimately prove more fiscally responsible than Lula would be in a fourth non-consecutive presidential term. However, markets are likely to give him the benefit of the doubt," said Thierry Larose, portfolio manager at Vontobel.
If he is elected, Bolsonaro would enjoy some room to maneuver with Congress after his Liberal Party emerged as the biggest winner in congressional races on Sunday.
Bolsonaro's party increased its representation in the Senate from 15 to 28 seats, the strongest result for a party since Brazil's return to democracy in 1985. It also is projected to secure 121 seats in the lower house, up from its current 98 seats.
"The likelihood of advancing reforms is much greater," said Pedro Paulo Silveira, an analyst at Terra Investimentos. He noted that during the previous Bolsonaro government, reforms often depended on costly political bargaining or stalled altogether.
Analysts also expect the real to continue strengthening into 2027. Societe Generale forecast that it would move to 5.10 by the end of 2026, with scope to move below 5.00 in the first half of 2027. Morgan Stanley forecast the real could strengthen past 4.90 and toward 4.50 in the first quarter of next year.
"The market wants change, it wants reform; it doesn't want a high public deficit; with the current government, all of this will continue," said Pedro Galdi, investment analyst at the AGF Investments platform.
Bolsonaro's strong showing is likely to boost market confidence in the near term, said Bryan Harris, a managing partner at Sabio.
"The market will be looking for clear signals from Bolsonaro that he is serious about tackling the country's problems," Harris said.
Heading into Sunday's vote, most private polls, which largely underestimated the younger Bolsonaro's strength, had shown the 45-year-old senator and Lula, who will turn 81 later this month, about even in a runoff vote.
Addressing a crowd at a hotel in Sao Paulo, Lula said he had been convinced he would win the election in the first round.
"Starting tomorrow, we begin a new campaign," the leftist leader said, promising to show voters what he had accomplished as president.

articles.title: Ukraine using AI-enabled robot guns to counter Russian drones
articles.summary: Ukraine commenced using artificial intelligence-enabled robot guns to bring down Russia's new and fast-moving jet-powered drones, according to its air force on Monday. For months,...
articles.full_text:
Ukraine commenced using artificial intelligence-enabled robot guns to bring down Russia's new and fast-moving jet-powered drones, according to its air force on Monday.
For months, Kyiv has been seeking a way to intercept the new Russian drones pounding the Ukrainian capital, even as it faces a dire lack of suitable ammunition to take them out.
Russia has been deploying newer jet-powered drones that move faster and are harder to intercept than the traditional models, which are based on Iranian Shahed drones.
As part of Ukraine's efforts to respond, "robotic turrets are now being installed on bridges," air force spokesperson Col. Yuri Ignat told national television.
"There have already been shoot downs," of the drones, including the bigger, faster and more powerful Geran-5 version, he told national television.
Speaking to Agence France-Presse (AFP), Ignat explained that the new turrets, which have been seen by AFP journalists in the Ukrainian capital, use "optical vision and artificial intelligence to eliminate the human factor and deliver strikes."
Sergiy Beskrestnov, a technology adviser to the Ukrainian defense ministry, explained on Telegram over the weekend that the new automated turrets were "an innovative Ukrainian solution that shoots down (drones) using machine guns controlled by artificial intelligence."
He said that 12 of the turrets had been installed in Kyiv, adding that "more turrets will be installed in the future."
Ignat acknowledged that the new system had a small operating radius.
"It can operate at about one kilometer plus (0.6 miles). And it works when conditions are favorable, when the attack approach angle is suitable," he told AFP.
"This is not some kind of panacea," he said, stressing that the turrets were part of "an integrated air defense system that provides engagement of these targets at different tiers."
"Of course, we rely on all available assets."
Ukraine has been accelerating the integration of artificial intelligence into its defense capabilities and is already using the technology on the frontlines to guide drones, detect targets for strikes and coordinate large-scale operations.

articles.title: Lithuania to prioritize security, competitiveness in EU presidency
articles.summary: Lithuania will put European security and economic competitiveness at the center of its upcoming EU presidency as the bloc navigates mounting geopolitical and economic uncertainty,...
articles.full_text:
Lithuania will put European security and economic competitiveness at the center of its upcoming EU presidency as the bloc navigates mounting geopolitical and economic uncertainty, President Gitanas Nauseda said Monday.
He met with Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis in Athens, with the two leaders addressing reporters after their talks.
Nauseda said his country’s presidency of the Council of the EU in the first half of 2027 was one of the main topics discussed.
"Europe faces security challenges and growing uncertainty. Therefore, our presidency will focus on making Europe stronger and more secure and increasing its competitiveness,” he said.
Mitsotakis said the leaders discussed the joint program of the EU presidency trio comprising Ireland, Lithuania, and Greece, according to Greek public broadcaster ERT.
He said the three countries shared a commitment to a free, democratic, strong, secure, prosperous, and competitive Europe.
The Greek prime minister stressed that defending the sovereignty and sovereign rights of EU and NATO members, particularly countries on the front line such as Lithuania and Greece, was a common responsibility.
Expressing Greece’s "absolute solidarity” with Lithuania over successive hybrid attacks, he called for a coordinated European response.
He also proposed developing joint European technologies to counter drones, stressing the need for more affordable ways to protect European airspace.
On migration, Mitsotakis said countries along the EU’s external borders must protect their borders while upholding their values and implementing the bloc’s Pact on Migration and Asylum.
Discussing negotiations on the EU’s next long-term budget, he said the resources initially proposed fell short of Europe’s growing ambitions, arguing that cohesion was a prerequisite for competitiveness.
Mitsotakis also reiterated support for a just and lasting peace in Ukraine that respects its sovereignty and territorial integrity and includes credible security guarantees.

articles.title: Russia quarantines dozens after Siberia plague researcher death
articles.summary: Russian authorities have quarantined dozens of people after a laboratory worker at a Siberian plague research institute died under undisclosed circumstances, prompting the head of...
articles.full_text:
Russian authorities have quarantined dozens of people after a laboratory worker at a Siberian plague research institute died under undisclosed circumstances, prompting the head of the national health watchdog to travel to the Irkutsk region.
The death has sparked public health fears on social media, but the authorities said Monday the situation was under control.
Plague is endemic to Siberia, location of the first known prehistoric human outbreak, as the bacterium that causes it, Yersinia pestis, is present among the small wild mammals in its vast wilderness and their fleas.
It is rare for Russians to fall ill with plague, however, though cases in other parts of the world – notably Africa – occur every year.
Local media named the woman as Darya Shipilova, an employee at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East.
There were conflicting reports about how and where the laboratory worker, whose age was given as 28, had fallen ill, but the authorities said she had died of pneumonia of as-yet unestablished origin.
Russia's health watchdog, Rospotrebnadzor, told state media the institute had not found evidence of any accidents involving the handling of pathogens after rumors spread on social media that the woman had dropped a test tube containing live bacteria.
Nevertheless, Anna Popova, the head of Rospotrebnadzor, flew to Siberia for an emergency meeting over the weekend.
An unspecified number of people who had been in contact with the dead woman were quarantined, parts of the hospital in the town of Shelekhov where she died were cordoned off, and an aluminum plant told its workers to wear masks.
Authorities urged people to remain calm and said there was no evidence that the woman's death was linked to her work.
Igor Kobzev, the governor of the Irkutsk region, said in a statement that she had died of "pneumonia of unknown aetiology," adding: "Importantly, over the past few days, no new cases of staff from the Anti-Plague Institute seeking medical attention have been identified."
He said the situation was under control and that all known contacts of the dead woman had been identified, examined and placed under medical supervision.
Plague comes in three forms affecting different parts of the body. Pneumonic plague, an infection of the lungs, prompts the patient to cough out infectious airborne droplets.
If identified quickly, it can be treated with antibiotics. But if left untreated, it can be fatal in one to six days.

articles.title: US withdraws all B-1 bombers from UK air base citing 'new threats'
articles.summary: The United States has withdrawn all B-1 bombers from RAF Fairford in Britain due to reported "new threats," though the British government insisted Monday the site is safe. Police w...
articles.full_text:
The United States has withdrawn all B-1 bombers from RAF Fairford in Britain due to reported "new threats," though the British government insisted Monday the site is safe.
Police were called to the base in southwest England on Sept. 27 after a local farmer reported a group of men with several vans engaged in "suspicious" activity.
The scare prompted a counterterrorism probe and forced evacuations at 85 homes near the airbase, which was used by the United States to launch strikes on Iran.
Investigators did not find any explosives in the vans, but "a quantity of petrol was recovered," according to counterterrorism police.
A statement from a Pentagon official Sunday said "we can acknowledge now that all U.S. bombers that were deployed to RAF Fairford have re-deployed to their home stations in the United States."
The statement noted that "operational security precluded us from confirming the movement of our assets and forces in real-time."
An unidentified U.S. official told CNN that the bombers were moved after "an unspecified new threat," with the source calling the latest threat a "real world incident."
It was unusual to move the bombers back to their home stations instead of deploying them to another base in the region, the official reportedly said.
Two U.S. officials told the New York Times that the bombers were moved after commanders received new threats about an Iran-backed plot against the base.
One American official said the new information was part of the same threat warnings that surfaced three weeks ago, but the situation became urgent in the past 24 hours, the Times reported.
Asked whether the base was safe, U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham's official spokesman said: "Yes."
"We have tried and tested approaches to defend our bases around the country and throughout the world," he told reporters.
Speculation about the motives behind the incident ranged from terror threat to fuel theft, as energy prices in the U.K. hit record highs this week.
Burnham has said there were "strong indications that Iran played a part" in the incident, a charge rejected by Tehran.
Six London-based Britons arrested in the September incident, including a U.K.-Iranian dual national, all men in their mid-20s, were released on bail, drawing rebuke from Washington.
"I wouldn't have done that," U.S. President Donald Trump told reporters, as his Secretary of State Marco Rubio alleged a "foreign actor" was involved.
Iran's embassy in London said it "categorically rejects and strongly condemns" speculation that Tehran was involved.
Adding to the mystery, British media reported that officers were alerted to the incident by one of the initial suspects, but police have not commented on the reports.
Security at the base had reportedly been heightened recently.
Britain gave Washington permission in March to use Fairford for "specific defensive operations into Iran," and U.S. bombers and other planes have since been seen taking off and landing at the base.
Fairford is the only airbase on Britain's mainland used for this purpose.
The incident came after a farmer living in the village of Whelford, near the airbase, called the police after seeing three vans blocking a road and a group of masked men fleeing the scene.
Aerial footage of the vans showed they appeared to contain barrels, and at least one was marked with a fake logo and phone number, giving the false impression that it was owned by a legitimate diesel delivery firm.

articles.title: Education disrupted as French high school protests enter 2nd week
articles.summary: Hundreds of high schools across France were fully or partially disrupted Monday as student protests over deteriorating education conditions continued, one day before a new nationwi...
articles.full_text:
Hundreds of high schools across France were fully or partially disrupted Monday as student protests over deteriorating education conditions continued, one day before a new nationwide mobilization called by student organizations and supported by several trade unions.
The Education Ministry said 413 establishments were affected by actions or disruptions Monday, including schools that had been closed.
The ministry said 40% of the establishments disrupted Monday had not been affected previously. Education Minister Edouard Geffray had said Sunday that classes would be totally or partially suspended in between 400 and 500 of France's roughly 3,700 high schools where security conditions could not be guaranteed.
The protests, which began at a school in the Paris region late September, have spread nationwide. Students have been protesting against teacher shortages and high rates of teacher absenteeism, overcrowded classrooms, poor school facilities and long school days. They have also raised concerns about inequalities associated with the Parcoursup university admissions platform.
Students in working-class suburbs have described the movement as a demand for equality, dignity and decent conditions for studying.
Sociologist Eric Fassin, a professor at Paris VIII University, told France 24 that he saw the student protests primarily as a demand for equality, dignity and recognition, with students seeking the basic conditions needed to study and have the same opportunities as students elsewhere.
The protests have also been marked by violent incidents and clashes with security forces. According to the Education Ministry, 24 schools have been burned or ransacked since the beginning of the movement.
More than 5,000 people have been arrested since the beginning of the movement; about 85% of them are minors.
In Belfort, eastern France, footage showing young people beating and kicking a police officer on the ground caused an outcry among officials.
Two Bulgarian nationals, aged 15 and 17, were arrested and investigated for suspected aggravated violence. One of them, whom the officer had attempted to arrest before the assault, subsequently filed a complaint alleging attempted murder through his lawyer.
The government's response has come under criticism from rights groups. Amnesty International's French branch accused police of using disproportionate violence and said students should be able to express their grievances without fear of being subjected to tear gas, batons or arbitrary detention.
Interior Minister Laurent Nunez rejected that criticism, saying security forces were not cracking down on young people but were protecting students who wished to express their demands peacefully.
Minister Geffray has said that activists, particularly from the far left, had infiltrated the student movement, "hijacked" it and engaged in extreme violence.
The government has announced measures aimed at addressing some of the students' demands. Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu has instructed local authorities to prioritize filling vacancies caused by long-term absences and unfilled posts. He has also scheduled a meeting with regional presidents to discuss the renovation of school buildings.
The organizers, however, have called for the protests to continue Tuesday, saying that the government has yet to propose concrete measures.
The CGT trade union has announced its participation in Tuesday's mobilization and said it would stand alongside the students. Several education unions have also called for participation. The Socialist Party has likewise called on its supporters to join the demonstrations.
The movement has also reached higher education. Higher Education and Research Minister Philippe Baptiste said he feared a national escalation involving universities and students.
He said between 30 and 40 higher education sites would be disrupted on Monday, either through blockades or administrative closures. Several university sites in Aix-en-Provence and Marseille were closed, and classes moved online.
Meanwhile, France's Senate is due to vote on Oct. 27 on a proposed law that would require protesters to pay for damage caused during demonstrations.
Under the proposal, an individual could be required to pay for damage without proof that they personally caused it, with the fine capped at 10,000 euros ($11,199).
